This page goes with **Chapter 24, Binary and Ternary Forms** of Robert Hutchinson's open textbook
[*Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom*](https://musictheory.pugetsound.edu/mt21c/BinaryAndTernaryForm.html). Read each section
there first. It uses [Chapter 13](phrases-in-combination.qmd) (phrases and cadences): the book writes **phrases in lowercase** (a, b) and
**sections in capitals** (A, B), and a section is usually one or more phrases.

The examples are a folk tune from the site's tune collection and two movements from the
[Analysed Scores Library](analysed-scores/view.qmd), where the experts' key labels sit under the music. The library's key plans are
read from the analysis data; its bar numbers are approximate (a few bars either way), so open the score and listen for the changes
yourself.

## 24.1 Sectional or continuous, and other descriptors

Every name for a binary or ternary form is built from descriptors in front of the form. The book gives these:

| Word | Means |
|---|---|
| **sectional** | the first section (A) ends on the **tonic chord** |
| **continuous** | the first section does **not** end on the tonic: it ends in a new key, or on a half cadence on V |
| **two-reprise** | both sections are repeated (the repeat signs are in the score) |
| **rounded** | the opening music comes back, after a contrasting passage, inside the second section |

So you might say "two-reprise continuous rounded binary". Say the descriptors first, the form last.
[Read 24.1](https://musictheory.pugetsound.edu/mt21c/BinaryAndTernaryForm.html)

A tune from the collection shows *sectional*: "Yankee Doodle" has two eight-bar sections, and the first ends on E♭, the tonic.

<div class="abc-ex" data-bpm="120"><script type="text/plain">
X:1
T:Yankee Doodle (Tune Library): A (bars 1-8) and B (bars 9-16)
M:2/4
L:1/8
Q:1/4=120
K:Eb
"Eb" EE FG | EG "Bb" FB, | "Eb" EE FG | E2 "Bb"D2 | "Eb" EE FG |"Ab" AG FE | "Bb" DB, CD | "Eb" E2 E2 ||
"Ab" C>D CB,| CD E2|"Eb" B,>C B,A, | G,2 B,2 | "Ab" C>D CB,| CD EC|"Eb" B,E "Bb"DF |"Eb"E2 E2|]
</script></div>

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answer

A ends on E♭ (bar 8: V to I with the melody on E♭), so the form is **sectional**. B is new music that also ends on the tonic. A does not
come back, so it is not rounded. It is a **sectional (simple) binary**, A B. Like a lot of folk music it is not a "binary" in the Baroque
sense of moving to V and back again.
:::

## 24.2 Three kinds of binary

**Balanced binary.** The first section ends in a new key (so it is continuous), and the second section ends with *essentially the same
cadence*, now in the home key. The book's examples are Bach's Invention No. 8 and the Courante of his French Suite No. 6, and the form is
common in Baroque dances.

**Rounded binary.** After a contrasting passage at the start of the second section, the **opening music of the first section returns**, often
shortened. It is common in Classical music (Haydn, Mozart, Beethoven), above all in a variation theme or the minuet of a minuet and trio.

**Simple binary.** Neither of the above: no matching endings and no return. The second section often *starts* like the first and then
develops its ideas. It is typical of Baroque and early Classical music.
[Read 24.2](https://musictheory.pugetsound.edu/mt21c/BinaryAndTernaryForm.html)

**The binary principle** is the key plan behind many Baroque binary pieces: the first section moves away from the tonic (to V in major,
to III in minor), the second moves back.

**Hear a rounded binary.** The minuet of Beethoven's first piano sonata is a clear one. Open
[Op. 2 No. 1, movement 3](analysed-scores/view.qmd?id=beethoven-sonata-1-3) (the library's version is in 3/4 and starts with the
minuet in F minor). The key labels in the analysis run **f minor, A♭ major, B♭ minor, f minor**: the first section leaves for the relative
major (so it is **continuous**), the second begins in a contrasting key (B♭ minor), and F minor, the opening key, is back
at about bar 19 (**rounded**). Play the library score from there and find the opening tune coming back.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself

The first section ends away from the tonic (A♭ major), the second section opens elsewhere and then returns to the tonic with the opening
melody. That is a **continuous rounded binary**; the repeats make it two-reprise. This is the reading the key plan supports; only your ears
can confirm the returning melody.
:::

## 24.3 Ternary form

Ternary form is **A B A**: statement, digression, restatement. Because the return is a full section, the B section is longer and more
independent than in rounded binary: in Romantic character pieces (nocturnes, intermezzos, songs without words) each section can run to more
than eight bars. The book's small example is Mozart's Andante K. 15mm, and its large one the Rachmaninov Prelude in C♯ minor.
[Read 24.3](https://musictheory.pugetsound.edu/mt21c/BinaryAndTernaryForm.html)

**Hear a ternary.** Mozart's Piano Sonata K. 545 has a slow movement with a clear contrasting middle.
[Open K. 545, movement 2](analysed-scores/view.qmd?id=mozart-sonata-16-2). The analysis's key labels run **G major, D major, G major,
G minor, B♭ major, C minor, G minor, G major**. The first stretch stays in G (with a side trip to D), the middle (from about bar 25) is
in the minor, and G major returns at about bar 37. A in the home key, B in the minor, A back: it is usually heard as a **sectional ternary**
(A closes in G). Listen for how different the B section's mood is.

A "compound ternary" is a ternary form in which one of the sections is itself binary or ternary. The book's examples are the minuet and
trio and the da capo aria. The whole of Beethoven's Op. 2 No. 1, III (above) is one: the minuet (rounded binary) is followed by a **trio** in
F major (the labels change to **F major, C major, F major** at about bar 30) and then the minuet again, from the start.

## 24.4 Rounded binary or ternary?

Pieces with five or six phrases can be either. The book offers three tests; weigh them, as they may not agree.

| Test | Points to rounded binary | Points to ternary |
|---|---|---|
| **Proportion** | the contrasting section is too short to stand alone (half as long as the opening, for example) | the middle section is as long as the others |
| **Nature** | built from the first section's motives; harmony mostly a dominant pedal or V alternating with I | a new, contrasting melody |
| **Era** | Baroque or Classical | Romantic |

[Read 24.4](https://musictheory.pugetsound.edu/mt21c/BinaryAndTernaryForm.html)

**Try it on the library.** Take Mozart's K. 545 slow movement and Beethoven's minuet above. For each: how long is the contrasting section
compared with the opening? Is its melody new, or a rearrangement of the opening? Which way do the three tests point? You will find they
point differently for the two, which is why the book calls this a judgment call.

## 24.5 Written-out repeats

Some pieces write the repeats out in full. Count them in your diagram (A A B B, not A B) even when the score doesn't show repeat signs.
[Read 24.5](https://musictheory.pugetsound.edu/mt21c/BinaryAndTernaryForm.html)

## 24.6 Real keyboard pieces to read

The site's full-score player has a set of short keyboard pieces from the Anna Magdalena Bach notebook and the early Mozart minuets. Their
notes were read bar by bar for this page, so the claims below can be checked by opening each score and following the bar numbers (a
pickup counts as bar 1). The scores are community engravings (see [the full scores page](analysed-scores/full-scores.qmd)), not a
printed edition, and the form names are this page's reading: **unverified** by an edition or a recording.

| Piece | Form (this page's reading) | What to look for |
|---|---|---|
| [Bach, Invention No. 8 in F, BWV 779](analysed-scores/full-scores.qmd?id=pdmx-84) | **balanced binary**, continuous | A (bars 1-11) ends on a C chord, the dominant; B (12-34) ends in F. Bars 30-33 are bars 8-11 again, note for note a fifth lower, and bar 34 is the last chord |
| [Mozart, Minuet in F, K. 5](analysed-scores/full-scores.qmd?id=pdmx-465) | **balanced binary**, continuous, two-reprise | A (1-10) ends in C; the music of bars 5-9 comes back a fifth lower, in F, in bars 15-19 |
| [Bach (Anh. 131), Gavotte in F](analysed-scores/full-scores.qmd?id=pdmx-490) | **simple binary**, continuous, two-reprise | A (1-8) ends on a C chord; B (9-17) is new and ends in F with different notes. Nothing returns |
| [Bach (Anh. 132), Minuet in D minor](analysed-scores/full-scores.qmd?id=pdmx-60) | **simple binary**, continuous, with **written-out repeats** | A (bars 1-8) closes in F major and is written twice (bars 9-16); B (17-24) is written twice (25-32) and ends in D minor. Put AABB in your diagram |
| [Haydn, Minuet, Hob. IX:8](analysed-scores/full-scores.qmd?id=pdmx-238) | **rounded binary**, sectional, two-reprise | A (1-9) ends on F, the tonic. B starts on a C pedal (bars 10-14), then bars 15-22 are bars 2-9 note for note |
| [Bach (Anh. 126), Musette in D](analysed-scores/full-scores.qmd?id=pdmx-23) | **rounded binary or ternary?** (see below) | A (1-8) is repeated; B (9-20) sits on a dominant pedal; A (21-28) comes back note for note |

**What was checked in the notes.** The matching of the repeats (the Invention's bars 30-33 against 8-11 (a fifth lower), the K. 5 minuet's bars 15-19 against 5-9 (a fifth lower), the Haydn minuet's bars 15-22
against 2-9, the Musette's bars 21-28 against 1-8) was checked by comparing the notes; the key and chord names (C chord, F major, dominant
pedal) were read from the bass notes and the key signature.

**The Musette, weighed with the three tests.** Proportion: B is 12 bars against A's 8, which points to ternary. Nature: mixed, since B is a new melody (ternary) but sits on a dominant pedal (E in the bass for bars 13-17), which the book reads as a sign of
rounded binary. Era: Baroque, which leans rounded binary. So the tests disagree. A teacher
could argue the other way, which is the point of the book's remark.

**Try it.** Open the Haydn minuet and the K. 5 minuet one after the other. Both have two repeated halves, and both A sections end away from
or on the tonic in different ways, but only one has the opening tune coming back in the second half. Which, and where?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## For teachers

- **Sources of the examples:** the tune is from the site's beginning-band set; the two movements are from the Analysed Scores Library
  (Mozart: DCML annotators' RomanText; Beethoven: BPS dataset). The key plans are read from the library's data; the bar numbers
  are approximate because the data places key changes at beat positions, not bar lines.
- **Readings of the forms** (continuous rounded binary for the Beethoven minuet, sectional ternary for the K. 545 slow movement) are
  this page's, from the key plans and general knowledge of the pieces; the book analyses other pieces. Checked against the library's key labels,
  not against a printed score.
- **The full-score pieces (24.6):** read from the notes in `apps/shared/data/full-scores/pdmx-<n>.abc` (made from PDMX community
  scores, converted and bar-checked by the PDMX pipeline). The form names are this page's reading, not checked against an edition. The
  Anh. numbers are from the scores' titles; I did not check them against the BWV Anhang catalogue.
- **Not here:** the book's own examples are mostly not in the collections (Brahms's Wiegenlied, Haydn Symphony No. 94 II, Mozart K. 15mm,
  Rachmaninov's prelude, Beethoven's Bagatelle Op. 119/9, Handel's Gavotte, the English Suite No. 3 gavotte: the PDMX conversion of that
  suite failed). The Courante of French Suite No. 6 is not there either.
- The text on this page is written for the site, not copied from the book (the book is under the GNU Free Documentation License).
